title: Rob the Houses of a Village Built as a Tree

concept.title: Tree DP: for every node keep the best sum with the node taken and with the node skipped
body: The houses of a village form a **tree**: the house 1 is the root, and every other house hangs from a parent with a smaller number. A thief may rob any set of houses, but **never a house together with its parent** (the two are linked by an alarm). What is the largest amount of money? Take the houses 2 and 3 hanging from the house 1 and the house 4 hanging from the house 2, with the money `3 4 5 1`: the best choice is the houses 2 and 3, 4 + 5 = 9.

This is the "no two neighbours" problem on a tree. For every house `v` keep two numbers about its **subtree** (the house and everything below it): `take[v]`, the best sum if `v` is robbed, and `skip[v]`, the best sum if `v` is not robbed. If `v` is robbed, its children must not be: `take[v] = money[v] + sum of skip[child]`. If `v` is not robbed, every child may be robbed or not, each independently: `skip[v] = sum of max(take[child], skip[child])`. The answer is `max(take[1], skip[1])`.

body.code:
take = money[:]                       # take[v]: money[v] + the skip values of the children so far
skip = [0] * n
for v in range(n - 1, 0, -1):        # children before parents: a parent has a smaller number
    p = parent[v] - 1
    take[p] += skip[v]
    skip[p] += max(take[v], skip[v])
print(max(take[0], skip[0]))

body: Because every parent has a smaller number than its children, going through the houses from the **last to the first** processes each house after all of its children, so no recursion is needed (a tree of 100 000 houses can be a chain that is too deep for recursion). The values of a house are final when the loop reaches it, and are then added to its parent. Time O(n), memory O(n).

statement: A village has `n` houses forming a tree rooted at the house 1; the parent of the house `v` (for `v >= 2`) has a smaller number than `v`. The house `v` holds `money[v]`. A thief may rob any set of houses in which no house is robbed together with its parent. Print the largest amount of money.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of houses (nodes) and `m = n - 1`.
The second line has `n` numbers: the money in each house (the houses are numbered from 1).
The third line has `m` numbers: for the houses 2, 3, ..., n, the number of the house they hang from. The parent of a house always has a smaller number.
outputFormat: Print the largest amount of money.

examples.note: The houses 2 and 3 (both hang from the house 1): 4 + 5 = 9.
The houses are linked: the richer one, 7.

hints: For each house keep the best sum of its subtree when the house is robbed and when it is not.
take[v] = money[v] + the skip values of the children; skip[v] = the sum of max(take, skip) of the children.
Go through the houses from the last to the first; every parent has a smaller number.

explanation: take[v] is the best sum of the subtree of v when v is robbed (its money plus the skip values of its children) and skip[v] when it is not (the sum of the better values of its children); going from the last house to the first processes every house after its children, and the answer is the larger value at the root.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
money = list(map(int, input().split()))
parent = list(map(int, input().split()))

take = money[:]
skip = [0] * n
for v in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
    p = parent[v - 1] - 1
    take[p] += skip[v]
    skip[p] += take[v] if take[v] > skip[v] else skip[v]
print(max(take[0], skip[0]))
